```{r}
#| label: load-packages-data
#| message: FALSE

library(shinydashboard)
library(haven)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(ggthemes)
library(forcats)
library(tidymodels)
library(plotly)


school_safety <- read_sas("data/pu_ssocs18.sas7bdat")
original_school_safety <- read_sas("data/pu_ssocs18.sas7bdat")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_family = "Atkinson Hyperlegible"))

# add the labels to a vector
# variable_labels_vector <- lapply(school_safety, function(var) attr(var, "label"))

```

```{r}
#| label: filter-data

# filter the data
# create final dataset to use

school_safety <- school_safety |>
  select(
    SCHID, # Unique school identifier
    INCPOL18, # Total number of incidents reported to police
    FR_URBAN, # Urbanicity - Based on urban-centric location of school
    FR_SIZE, # Size of school
    C0110:C0186, # School Practices and Programs 
    C0600,
    C0604:C0610,
    C0190:C0192,
    C0204:C0218,
    C0610:C0650,
    C0661,
    C0667,
    C0266:C0277, # Teacher Training
    OUTSUS18 # Suspensions
  )

school_safety <- school_safety |>
  mutate_at(
    vars(starts_with("C")), ~ str_replace(., "2", "0"), 
    vars(starts_with("C")), ~ str_replace(., "-1", "0")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(starts_with("C"), as.numeric),
    resource_sum = 
           C0183 + C0181 + C0179 + C0186 + C0604 + C0606 + C0608 + C0190 + 
           C0192 + C0204 + C0206 + C0208 + C0210 + C0212 + C0214 + C0216 + 
           C0218 + C0266 + C0268 + C0265 + C0267 + C0269 + C0270 + C0272 + 
           C0278 + C0271 + C0273 + C0274 + C0276 + C0277 + C0610,
  ) |>
  arrange(resource_sum) 

```

```{r}
#| label: linear-regressions-for-each-resource

name <- colnames(school_safety |>
  select(starts_with("C")))

# create a vector to store all the values of the r-squared coefficients
r_squared_values <- numeric()
slope <- numeric()

# calculate all the r_squared values for every resource
for (variable in name) {
  # Fit a simple linear regression model for each predictor variable
  lm_model <- lm(school_safety$INCPOL18 ~ factor(school_safety[[variable]])
                 + school_safety$FR_SIZE
                )
  # Calculate the R-squared value
  r_squared <- summary(lm_model)$r.squared
  tidy_slope <- tidy(lm_model)|>
    filter(term == "factor(school_safety[[variable]])1")
  slope_value <- tidy_slope$estimate
  # Append values to the vectors
  slope <- c(slope, slope_value)
  r_squared_values <- c(r_squared_values, r_squared)
}

# assign all vectors to the resource regression dataframe
resource_regressions2 <- data.frame(name = name, 
                                    slope = slope, 
                                    r_squared_val = r_squared_values
                                    )

```

# Home

## Column

```{r}
#| label: scatter plot resources v. incidents all schools
#| fig-alt: |
#|   The graph is a jittered scatter plot titled, “Effect of School Resources on
#|   Incidents Reported to Police.” The x axis is “Amount of School
#|   Resources (out of 30)” and the y axis is “Total Number of Incidents
#|   Reported to the Police.” The x-axis ranges from 0 to 30, and the y
#|   axis ranges from 0 to about 350. The points are clustered close to
#|   the x axis, with most of the points being below 100 incidents
#|   reported to police, though there are some outliers above this line. Most 
#|   notably, there is one point located at 29 resources and 325 incidents 
#|   reported to police. There are also more points clustered between 10 and 30
#|   school resources compared to below 10 and over 30 (the points above 30 are 
#|   due to the degree od variability that results from using the geom_jitter function). 
#|   There appears to be a slight positive trend, with incidents reported to police increasing 
#|   as amount of school resources increases, though it is very slight and difficult to
#|   discern. The shape of the distribution is a very slight left skew.

# all schools
school_safety |>
  ggplot(aes(x = resource_sum, y = INCPOL18)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of School Resources on Incidents Reported to Police", 
    x = "Amount of School Resources (out of 30)",
    y = "Total Number of Incidents Reported to the Police"
  ) 

```

## Column {.tabset}

```{r}
#| label: Bar graph comparing incidents to school size
#| title: Total Incidents Between School Size
#| fig-alt: |
#|    This graph is a bar plot titled "Average Incidents Per School Compared to
#|    School Size" The x axis is "School Size" with four categories, each with
#|    their own bar: "< 300," "300 - 499," "500 - 999," and ">= 1000." The y axis
#|    is "Average Incidents Per School," ranging from 0 to about 30. The
#|    furthest-left bar, the "> 300" bar, is solid from 0 to about 3. The second
#|    bar from the left, the "300 - 499" bar, is solid from 0 to about 4. The
#|    third bar from the left, the "500 - 999" bar, is solid from 0 to about 12.
#|    The furthest-right bar, the ">=1000" bar is solid from 0 to about 27.

school_safety |>
  group_by(FR_SIZE) |>
  summarize(average_incidents_per_school = mean(INCPOL18)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(FR_SIZE), y = average_incidents_per_school, fill = FR_SIZE)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Incidents Per School Compared to School Size", 
    x = "School Size", 
    y = "Average Incidents Per School"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("< 300", "300 - 499", "500 - 999", ">= 1000")) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 30), breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r}
#| label: interactive-plot
#| title: School Resources and Practices
#| fig-alt: |
#|   The graph is a bar plot titled, “School Resources and Practices Impact
#|   on Incidents Reported to Police.” The x axis contains the variable
#|   names of 91 school resources, while the y axis is the slope of each
#|   variable. Each variable has its own colored bar that visualizes its
#|   slope compared to the other variables. Most of the variables have
#|   slopes between 0 and 10, although there are 22 variables with negative
#|   slopes, and 12 variables with slopes above 10. When the cursor of
#|   the computer is hovered over a bar, the variable name and slope will
#|   appear. The four variables with clearly strong slopes are C0110, with a
#|   slope of -3.367, C0153, with a slope of -3.769, C0604, with a slope of
#|   9.054, and C0646, with a slope of 9.357. The colors of the bars
#|   correlate to the R-values of the variables, with a scale ranging from
#|   light blue to dark blue visualizing this. Variables with the lowest 
#|   R-values are colored lighter blue, while variables with the highest 
#|   R-values are colored darker blue.


plot_ly(data = resource_regressions2, 
        x = ~name, 
        y = ~slope, 
        type = 'bar', 
        text = ~paste("Variable: ", name, "<br>Slope: ", slope),
        hoverinfo = 'text', 
        marker = list(color = ~r_squared_val, colorscale = 'Blues')) |>
  layout(title = "School Resources and Practices Impact on Incidents 
         Reported to Police"
         )
```

# C0648: Law Enforcement Officer for Instructional Hours

## Column

```{r}
#| label: Law-Officers-Present-Vary-with-Incidents
#| fig-alt: |
#|   The graph is a bar plot titled, “Average Incidents for Schools With and 
#|   Without LGBTQ Acceptance Groups.” The x axis is “Has LGBTQ 
#|   Acceptance Groups” with the left bar labeled “No” and the right bar 
#|   labeled “Yes.” The y axis is “Average Incidents Per School” and ranges 
#|   from 0 to about 25. The left bar, the “No” bar, is filled in 
#|   to about 7, and the right bar, the “Yes” bar, is filled in to about 22.
#|   The bars are different colors to provide contrast. 

school_safety$C0562 <- as.factor(original_school_safety$C0562)

school_safety <- school_safety |>
  mutate(C0648 = as.factor(C0648))

school_safety |>
  group_by(C0648) |>
  summarize(average_incidents_per_school = mean(INCPOL18)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = C0648, y = average_incidents_per_school, fill = C0648)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  labs(title = "Sworn Law Enforcement Officer Present for All Instructional Hours \nVersus Average Incidents Reported to Police In Schools", 
       x = "Presence of Sworn Law Enforcement Officers All Instructional Hours",
       y = "Average Incidents Reported to the Police per School") + 
  #scale_x_discrete(labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_colorblind()
```

## Column {.tabset}

```{r}
#| label: Law-Officers-Present-Vary-with-Crime
#| title: Crime
#| fig-alt: |
#|   The graph is a segmented bar plot titled, “Impact of LGBTQ Acceptance
#|   Groups on Incidents Reported to Police by School Size.” The x axis is
#|   “School Size,” with four different categories: “> 300,” “300 - 499,”
#|   “500 - 999,” and “1000+.” The y axis is “Percentage of Incidents
#|   Reported to Police” and ranges from 0.00 to 1.00. Color is used in this
#|   plot to represent “Presence of LGBTQ Acceptance Groups.” For each of
#|   the school size categories, there is a full bar going from 0.00 - 1.00,
#|   with the bottom of the bar being blue, to represent “Yes,” and the top
#|   of the bar being red to represent “No.” This visualizes each school
#|   size category’s proportion of incidents reported to police based on
#|   whether or not LGBTQ Acceptance Groups are present. The blue portion of
#|   the left-most bar, the “> 300” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.35. The
#|   red portion of this bar goes from about 0.35 to 1.00. The blue portion
#|   of the second bar from the left, the “300 - 499” bar, goes from 0.00 to
#|   about 0.20 and the red portion goes from about 0.20 to 1.00. The blue
#|   portion of the third bar from the left, the “500 - 999” bar, goes from
#|   0.00 to about 0.30 and the red portion goes from about 0.30 to 1.00.
#|   The blue portion of the most-right bar, the “1000+” bar, goes from 0.00
#|   to about 0.85, and the red portion goes from about 0.85 to 1.00.


# crime graph
ggplot(school_safety, aes(x = fct_rev(C0562), y = INCPOL18, fill = C0648)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Sworn Law Enforcement Officer Present for All Instructional Hours \nVersus Crime in School Area",
    x = "Crime in School Area",
    y = "Incidents Reported to Police",
    fill = "Presence of Sworn Law Enforcement Officers All Instructional Hours"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")) +
 # scale_fill_manual(values = c("#F2BB9B", "#03658C")) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom") +
  scale_fill_colorblind(labels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

```{r}
#|   bar being red to represent “No.” This visualizes each school size
#|   category’s proportion of incidents reported to police based on whether
#|   or not School Uniforms are required. The blue portion of the left-most
#|   bar, the “> 300” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.39. The red portion of
#|   this bar goes from about 0.39 to 1.00. The blue portion of the second
#|   bar from the left, the “300 - 499” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.20
#|   and the red portion goes from about 0.20 to 1.00. The blue portion of
#|   the third bar from the left, the “500 - 999” bar, goes from 0.00 to
#|   about 0.19 and the red portion goes from about 0.19 to 1.00. The blue
#|   portion of the most-right bar, the “1000+” bar, goes from 0.00 to about
#|   0.06, and the red portion goes from about 0.06 to 1.00.

# crime graph
ggplot(school_safety, aes(x = fct_rev(C0562), y = INCPOL18, fill = C0110)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Required Visitor Check In and Badges \nVersus Crime in School Area",
    x = "Crime in School Area",
    y = "Incidents Reported to Police",
    fill = "Required Visitor Check In and Badges"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom") +
  scale_fill_colorblind(labels = c("No", "Yes"))

```

```{r}
#| label: Visitor-Check-In-Vary-with-urbanicity

#|   axis is “Urbanicity,” with four different categories: “City,” “Suburb,”
#|   “Town,” and “Rural.” The y axis is “Percentage of Incidents Reported to
#|   Police” and ranges from 0.00 to 1.00. Color is used in this plot to
#|   represent “Required School Uniforms.” For each of the school size
#|   categories, there is a full bar going from 0.00 - 1.00, with the bottom
#|   of the bar being blue, to represent “Yes,” and the top of the bar being
#|   red to represent “No.” This visualizes each school urbanicity
#|   category’s proportion of incidents reported to police based on whether
#|   or not School Uniforms are required. The blue portion of the left-most
#|   bar, the “City” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.18. The red portion of
#|   this bar goes from about 0.18 to 1.00. The blue portion of the second
#|   bar from the left, the “Suburb” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.10 and
#|   the red portion goes from about 0.10 to 1.00. The blue portion of the
#|   third bar from the left, the “Town” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.11
#|   and the red portion goes from about 0.11 to 1.00. The blue portion of
#|   the most-right bar, the “Rural” bar, goes from 0.00 to about 0.06, and
#|   the red portion goes from about 0.06 to 1.00.

#urbanicity graph
ggplot(school_safety, aes(x = as.factor(FR_URBAN), y = INCPOL18, fill = C0110)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Required Visitor Check In and Badges \nVersus School Urbanicity",
    x = "School Urbanicity",
    y = "Incidents Reported to Police",
    fill = "Required Visitor Check In and Badges"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("City", "Subruban", "Town", "Rural")) +
  theme(legend.position="bottom") +
  scale_fill_colorblind(labels = c("No", "Yes"))
```
